items.title: A high level introduction to Diffusion Models
items.content_html:
This article is a high level overview of diffusion models (for image generation). We will not be getting into the mathematical basis of the models here (You can refer to this excellent article for an in-depth introduction to diffusion models), or the nitty-gritty impelementation details (which you can find here).

What are diffusion models?

Diffusion models are neural networks that generate samples similar to a set of input images by incrementally adding noise to them and learning to denoise them.

In the above image, q is the forward process and our model is used to approximate the reverse process. Instead of modeling the inversion distribution function, the model estimates the noise that is added in the forward process. The loss is accordingly rewritten in terms of the predicted noise. The architecture used is a modified U-net model (Ronneburger et al.), with attention modules added before the downsampling and upsampling steps. 

The model learns how to denoise an image and after all time steps, it maps into the distribution of the training dataset. To generate a novel sample from the data distribution of the training data, we can use randomly generated array of pixel values and pass it to the model to get a new sample.

Faster inference in diffusion models

Diffusion models were introduced in the paper by Ho et al. (2020) titled Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM). Song et al. (2020) improved upon their model in their paper titled Denoising Diffusion Implicit Model (DDIM). 

The key idea of the paper was formulating a non-markovian sampling strategy that results in the same variational lower bound objective. The forward process remains the same while the reverse process can be done using a shorter sampling trajectory. The reverse process in DDPM involves sampling from a distribution involving the previous sample and the estimated noise given by the weights. Thus, we will need to generate samples for the every intermediate timestep to get a novel sample from the dataset. Sampling method in DDIM is deterministic, given the value at the previous time step in the trajectory, we use the estimate of the final sample (x₀)  and the denoising predicted by the model at that point to generate the sample at the current step. This allows us to generate samples using an arbitrary number of time-steps. The authors find that at shorter timesteps (~50), DDIM generates an image close to the image found at the 500th/1000th timestep.

In addition, since the process is deterministic, given the same starting sample, we will generate the same final image. Therefore, it also induces a latent space in the input sample space. Given two outputs of the DDIM procedure, we can generate an output that is a combination of the features of the two images by interpolating their inputs.

Improving the model

We highlight the key contributions of the paper Improved Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (IDDPM) by Nichol and Dhariwal (2021). A key distinction that needs to be made here is the difference between the noise schedule and the variance schedule. Noise schedule controls the rate of addition of noise in the forward process. In the reverse process, we also model it as a gaussian. The selected variance of the reverse process is dictated by the variance schedule. Why do they need to be different? We want our model to approximate the true posterior of the intermediate values of the reverse process. The last step's posterior should be the same as the training data distribution. This is an intractable distribution, it's variance depends on the dataset and therefore, does not have to equal the variance of the forward process. The authors of DDPM experimented with two choices of variance in the reverse process:

  1. Setting it to be the same as the variance in the forward process
  2. Deriving the mathematical form of the true posterior, conditioned on x₀ (true posterior unconditioned on x₀ is what we want our model to approximate) , and setting the variance equal to it's variance.

The authors found that they resulted in similar results with either of these choices. IDDPM improves this by setting a trainable parameter that interpolates these two variances. This results in model flexibility and when optimized, a closer approximation to the true posterior distribution. The authors have also experimented with a different noise schedule, where they use a cosine schedule where the variance is more gradually increased closer to t = 0 and t = T (as illustrated below). Note that the graph depicts ⍺, which is inversely related to the variance β = 1 - ⍺. 

Introducing Guidance

DDPM provides no control on the outputs of the model, except that outputs will belong to the training dataset. DDIM gives one level of additional control because of the induced latent space in the input (noise). There are two approaches to adding more control: Classifier guided models and Classifier-free models.

Classifier Guidance

This method involves training a classifier on noisy images and the diffusion models separately. During inference, the gradient of log-likelihood of the noisy intermediate samples are used to drive the update towards the desired class.

Classifier-free Guidance

In Classifier-free guidance, we add the class information as input to the model and train a model that learns class conditioned diffusion and unconditional diffusion jointly. We train with a fraction of samples pdrop having a null-token as the class information (to learn unconditional generation) and the rest with encoded class information. During inference, a parameter w called guidance strength controls how strongly the user input guides the model, resulting in a controllable trade-off between sample diversity and adherence to inputs.

As we see in the update equation above, a higher w results in stronger adherence to the user-input class information and a lower w results in images closer to the training data distribution.

items.title: LoRA: paper explained
items.content_html:
Alternatively, Understanding intrinsic dimension of LLM models and its implications.

Here I will be giving you a breakdown of the seminal paper LoRA: Low-rank adaptation of large language models by Hu et al. (2021) at Microsoft. The paper tackles a critical problem faced in practical uses of LLMs — expensive compute of fine-tuning large language models. First, I will introduce the related work done prior to the paper highlighting the key ideas which directly lead to the method used in LoRA. Next, I will explain the method introduced by this paper and go over the conclusions presented.

 

Intrinsic Dimension of a model

The concept of intrinsic dimension of a model was introduced in the paper Measuring the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes by Li et al. (2018). The paper explores what the minimum number of parameters required are for a given loss function (or objective landscape). Let’s say we’re trying to find the optimal solution with D parameters θ*ᴰ for a loss function, then its intrinsic dimension dᵢₙₜ is the D-s, where s is the dimension of the subspace of the optimal solutions. For example, we pick an optimization problem where the loss is (x₁ — 1)² + (x₂ — 1)² and we try to find the solution in a ten dimensional parameter space. We will have a solution manifold of dimension 8 since coordinates x₃ through x₁₀ can be varied independently without affecting the loss. Hence the intrinsic dimension is 2. In our toy example it was easy to find the intrinsic dimension because the loss function was simple. In day-to-day ML applications, we cannot find the closed box formula for the optimal solution and thereby find the intrinsic dimension. In such cases, we define the best possible baseline solution we can find thorough fine-tuning as the baseline solution and its number of parameters as the intrinsic dimension. We define dᵢₙₜ₉₀ as the intrinsic dimension which can give us 90% of the performance of this baseline solution. The results shown in the paper point to neural networks being highly compressible, with dᵢₙₜ₉₀ being much lower than the baseline intrinsic dimension dᵢₙₜ₁₀₀. So, how exactly do we find dᵢₙₜ₉₀ for a neural network when we have our objective function defined in D parameters? We use a method to project a lower dimension parameter θᵈ to D parameters, such as multiplying it by a (random, fixed) Dxd matrix and optimizing the resulting loss landscape. We increase the dimension d until we hit a point where we get 90% of the performance of the baseline and this will be dᵢₙₜ₉₀. The paper explores other projection methods as well, such as using the Fastfood transform, which has better space and time complexities for projecting a vector into higher dimensions. The Fastfood transform is used extensively in the paper we discuss in the next section.

 

Intrinsic Dimension of adjustments in LLM fine-tuning

This paper by Aghajanyan et al. (2020) explores the intrinsic dimensionality of the fine-tuning adjustments in LLMs instead of the intrinsic dimensionality of the whole model which was explored by the paper discussed above. LLMs characteristically have a large number of parameters and therefore, fine-tuning the entire model requires a lot of compute. Say we have a pre-trained LLM model with D parameters. For a downstream task such as a binary classification predicting semantic equality of two text bodies/phrases, we compute dᵢₙₜ₉₀ by projecting the parameters to D parameters using the Fastfood Transform as illustrated below:

We defer digression about the projection matrix M, as we shall discuss the implications of the method rather than its intricacies itself. Keep in mind that M is a matrix that is randomly generated at the start and remains fixed while we optimize θᵈ.
Note that, naturally, we are only restricting the number of parameters in the fine tuning space using the above equation and the method of loss computation remains unchanged. This method is agnostic of the layered structure of LLMs, where each layer has a specialized purpose. Thus, to tackle this, another method proposed in the paper:

where we trade off m parameters (where m is the number of layers in the LLM) towards scaling the layer-specific parameters. The intrinsic dimension found this way is named the Structure-Aware Intrinsic Dimension (SAID). Alternatively, the intrinsic dimension found using the other method which is structure agnostic is called Direct Intrinsic Dimension (DID). The experiments done indicate that SAID is typically lower than DID. The crucial takeaways from the paper are that both SAID & DID (for 90% of the baseline performance) are much lower than the number of parameters and that the intrinsic dimension decreases as the size of the pre-trained model increases. The latter result makes sense since the larger pre-trained model “understands” the language better, therefore achieving competitive performance on the downstream tasks is relatively easier. To summarize, we have observed that we can reach competitive performance in LLM fine-tuning by using lower dimensional parameters. Note that we are still using the Fastfood transform to project these into the full model parameter sized space, where we have a fixed, randomly-generated projection matrix. Can we do better than this? Let’s find out…

 

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)

Finally we come to the main paper which has seen widespread usage and has lead to a proliferation in fine-tuned models, LoRA. The above papers discuss the concept of intrinsic dimension of the models and the update parameters in model fine-tuning. This inspires the main hypothesis of the paper: that the update weight matrices in these models are of a low “intrinsic rank” and hence can be modeled by rank-decomposition matrices whose parameters are fully trainable! Let us denote the pre-trained weight matrix as W₀ and the update matrix for it as ΔW. Then we have the mathematical description below for model fine-tuning weight update:

where B and A are trainable matrices. Matrix A is initialized by random Gaussian sampling and B is initialized to a zero matrix.

Applying LoRA to transformers

We have described the basic idea of LoRA above. How do we apply it to transformer models? The transformer models have several trainable parameters such as the query matrix Wq, key matrix Wk, value matrix Wv and the output projection matrix in multi-head attention models Wo for each layer. In addition there is a feed-forward layer with weights Wd. The approach in the paper uses independent LoRA matrix pairs for each matrix in the attention heads and leaves the feed-forward matrices unchanged. That’s it! This is a simple and straightforward method that is inspired by the previous works and improves upon them substantially.

What is the optimal r to be used in the weight matrices? The experimental results show that we improve upon the performance of fine-tuning the full model (Previous papers find dᵢₙₜ₉₀ which reaches 90% of this performance) with r being as little as 1 or 2! Further increases in r don’t result in significant gains and in some cases reduce the performance as well.

There are numerous advantages to using LoRA in LLMs. For a given downstream task, we can pre-compute the adapted weights by adding up the update matrices to the pre-trained models and thus have no additional inference latency, as opposed to some other methods such as introducing adapter layers which increases the latency. We can store the fine-tuned models for several downstream tasks by storing the pre-trained model and only the LoRA update matrices for each respective task (which are much smaller than the model). As r is increased to the rank of the optimal update matrices of the full model (including the feed-forward layer matrices and their biases), we will reach the expressiveness of fine-tuning the full model. Thus, LoRA can be seen as a generalization of full fine-tuning a model.

 

Thanks for reading! Please feel free to let me know if there are any mistakes above or if you have any questions in the response section below. Also, let me know if you have any suggestions for what paper I can explain next!
